articles.title: Designing a Mobile-Friendly Contact Flow for a Small-Business Website
articles.excerpt: A contact button is only one part of a contact flow. Visitors also need to understand what will happen, the interaction needs to work on a phone, and the business needs a reliable way to respond. Here…
articles.body: A contact button is only one part of a contact flow. Visitors also need to understand what will happen, the interaction needs to work on a phone, and the business needs a reliable way to respond. Here is a platform-independent way to design and test that flow. Start with one action List the actions a visitor might take: send a message, call, request a quote, or submit a form. Pick the primary action for the page and make it visually clear. Secondary options can remain available without competing for attention. Use labels that describe the result. “Ask about a project” is more specific than “Submit.” Make links behave like links For navigation to another page or service, use a real anchor with a descriptive destination.
articles.author: Tarraqix

articles.title: Guardrail independente de modelo
articles.excerpt: Resposta curta Guardrail independente de modelo é uma camada de segurança que opera fora do ciclo de inferência do modelo de IA, aplicando regras, filtros e validações padronizadas independentemente d…
articles.body: Resposta curta Guardrail independente de modelo é uma camada de segurança que opera fora do ciclo de inferência do modelo de IA, aplicando regras, filtros e validações padronizadas independentemente da arquitetura, tamanho ou fornecedor do modelo subjacente. Essa abordagem permite governança consistente em ambientes multimodelo — como LLMs de diferentes famílias (Granite, Llama, Mistral) — sem necessidade de reconfiguração por modelo. TL;DR Funciona como middleware ou proxy entre entrada do usuário e saída do modelo, sem alterar os pesos ou a inferência. Suporta políticas baseadas em regex, classificação de conteúdo, verificação de PII, regras lógicas e RAG-augmented validation.

articles.title: Enhancing FastAPI Request Parameters with Pydantic Validation Options
articles.excerpt: Why Fine-Grained Validation on Request Parameters Matters When building modern APIs, validating incoming request data is crucial to ensure correctness, security, and maintainability. FastAPI, renowned…
articles.body: Why Fine-Grained Validation on Request Parameters Matters When building modern APIs, validating incoming request data is crucial to ensure correctness, security, and maintainability. FastAPI, renowned for its seamless integration with Pydantic, already offers powerful data validation for request bodies. However, until recently, its support for expressive validation on request parameters — such as query strings, path variables, or headers — was limited to basic type checks. This gap meant developers often had to add extra manual validation or rely on less idiomatic workarounds. This article dives into a recent improvement in FastAPI that unlocks the full power of Pydantic's validation options for request parameters.
articles.author: Priyadarshan Singh

articles.title: Building an AI phone caller that has to admit it's an AI: what 26 real calls broke
articles.excerpt: I built Arogo, a small service where you type a question for a business ("does the vet take new patients, and what's a first visit?"), approve a plan, and a voice agent phones them and sends you the a…
articles.body: I built Arogo, a small service where you type a question for a business ("does the vet take new patients, and what's a first visit?"), approve a plan, and a voice agent phones them and sends you the answer plus the whole transcript. The stack is boring on purpose: a Node server, a voice-agent platform for the call itself, a phone number, and an LLM that writes the plan. The interesting part is everything that went wrong on real phone lines. We ran 26 real calls over two days. 12 businesses answered the question, 9 hung up on the AI, and 5 couldn't be reached. Here's what broke and what we changed. 1. The model hangs up after pressing a key Phone menus ("press 2 for appointments") were the first thing to kill calls.

articles.body: Claude Code finishes a change. The project builds. The tests pass. You still do not know whether the screen works. articles.title: Work Permit Expired? A Restoration of Status Checklist for Tech Workers in Canada
articles.excerpt: A missed work-permit deadline can turn an ordinary employment issue into an urgent immigration problem. If a Canadian work permit expires before a valid extension application is submitted, the worker…
articles.body: A missed work-permit deadline can turn an ordinary employment issue into an urgent immigration problem. If a Canadian work permit expires before a valid extension application is submitted, the worker may lose both temporary resident status and authorization to work. This checklist is for developers, engineers, product professionals and other technology workers. It provides general information, not individual legal advice. 1. Confirm the actual expiry date Read the permit itself. The expiry date is normally when the person must stop working. If the document contains a separate “Must leave Canada by” date, that date may control when temporary resident status expires. Do not rely only on an employer reminder, calendar entry, visa counterfoil or passport stamp.

articles.title: What exactly is a light-day? Here's what Voyager 1's latest milestone means for the interstellar probe
articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 is approaching a distance of one light-day from Earth, a milestone that highlights the enormous distances involved in deep-space exploration.
articles.body: After nearly 50 years traveling through space, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a milestone no human-made object has reached before: a distance of one light-day from Earth. This milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (1016:07 GMT) — highlights the immense distances Voyager 1 has traveled and the challenges of communicating with spacecraft operating in the outer reaches of the solar system and beyond. Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours. Light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second, meaning one light-day is roughly 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), according to a statement from NASA.

articles.title: The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18! Here's what you need to know
articles.excerpt: The Leonid meteor shower peaks overnight on Nov. 17-18, sending shooting stars racing across the night sky from the direction of the constellation Leo.
articles.body: The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18 sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation . NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell. Leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026!

articles.title: Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years
articles.excerpt: The legend of the Black Knight satellite offers an example of how a collection of unconnected events and speculative interpretations can accumulate into a single conspiracy theory over time.
articles.body: In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station , crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space. Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction.
